title: Review: Catalysis (homogeneous and heterogeneous); Dynamic equilibrium and Kc expressions; Le Chatelier and industrial compromise
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EQ01#t3 term and clue written for the game; EQ02#t4 term and clue written for the game; EQ01#t1 term and clue written for the game; EQ02#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EQ01#N.13, EQ02#N.14, KN08#N.14, EQ01#N.12, EQ02#N.10, KN08#N.7, EQ01#N.8a, EQ02#N.7a, KN08#N.6a, EQ01#N.10a, EQ02#N.12, EQ01#N.6. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Closed system
items.clue: A set-up in which nothing enters or leaves.

items.label: Equilibrium constant
items.clue: The value K, which only a change in temperature can alter.

items.label: Reversible reaction
items.clue: A chemical change that can go both ways, shown with the symbol ⇌.

items.label: Le Chatelier's principle
items.clue: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts so as to partly oppose the change.

questions.stem: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine can be kept in the dark for days with no visible change. Yet for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ 2HCl(g), K ≈ 2 × 10³³ at 298 K. What do these facts tell you?

options.text: At equilibrium it would be mostly H₂ and Cl₂, because no HCl forms in the dark.
It is already at equilibrium, because nothing changes while it is in the dark.
At equilibrium it would be almost all HCl; in the dark it reacts extremely slowly.
It must react quickly in the dark, because a very large K means a fast reaction.

questions.explanation: K ≫ 1, so the equilibrium lies far to the right. K tells you how far, not how fast: in the dark the reaction is too slow to see.

questions.stem: Methanol is made from CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. Plants run it at high pressure. Why does raising the pressure, by reducing the volume, increase the equilibrium yield of methanol?

options.text: K increases at high pressure, so more methanol is present at equilibrium.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so high pressure pushes the position right.
The position shifts right: the right side has fewer moles of gas.
More frequent collisions at high pressure speed up the forward reaction only.

questions.explanation: 3 mol of gas on the left, 1 on the right. Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, which partly opposes the change.

questions.stem: High in the atmosphere, chlorine atoms destroy ozone in two steps. Overall: O₃ + O → 2O₂. Which statement is correct? Step 1: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂. Step 2: ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂.

options.text: ClO is the catalyst, as it is formed in one step and used up in the next.
O₃ is the catalyst, as it reacts in the first step.
Cl and ClO are both catalysts, as neither appears in the overall equation.
Cl is the catalyst and ClO is an intermediate.

questions.explanation: Cl joins in, changes to ClO, then comes back as Cl, ready to go round again.

questions.stem: CO₂(g) + H₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂O(g). The forward reaction is endothermic. Which change increases the value of Kc?

options.text: Adding more H₂ at constant temperature
Raising the pressure at constant temperature
Adding a catalyst
Raising the temperature

questions.explanation: Only temperature changes Kc. The forward reaction is endothermic, so Kc increases as the temperature rises.

questions.stem: A test tube holds orange potassium dichromate(VI) solution: 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). Sodium hydroxide solution is added drop by drop. What is seen, and why?

options.text: It turns yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the position shifts left.
There is no change, because OH⁻ does not appear in the equation.
It turns a deeper orange, because the added base speeds up the forward reaction.
It turns yellow, because the alkali lowers the value of K.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ reacts with H⁺ to form water. Losing H⁺ shifts the position left, towards yellow chromate(VI).

questions.stem: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Which statement is correct?

options.text: It gives a fast enough rate at a lower temperature, saving energy and CO₂ emissions.
It increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia by shifting the equilibrium to the right.
It is a homogeneous catalyst, as it is in the same reactor as the gases.
It is used up as the reaction proceeds, so it must be added in a fixed mole ratio to N₂.

questions.explanation: Lower Ea means a useful rate without extra heating: less fuel burned, lower costs, less CO₂.

questions.stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). At equilibrium, [N₂] = 0.50, [H₂] = 0.40 and [NH₃] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³. What is Kc?

options.text: 0.36 mol² dm⁻⁶
1.5 dm³ mol⁻¹
2.8 dm⁶ mol⁻²
2.8 mol² dm⁻⁶

questions.explanation: Kc = 0.30² ÷ (0.50 × 0.40³) = 0.090 ÷ 0.032 = 2.8. Units: (mol dm⁻³)² ÷ (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻² = dm⁶ mol⁻².

questions.stem: The forward reaction in the following equilibrium is exothermic: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased at constant pressure. How do the amount of SO₃ and the value of K at the new equilibrium compare with those at the original equilibrium?

options.text: A larger amount of SO₃ and a larger value of K.
A smaller amount of SO₃ and a smaller value of K.
An unchanged amount of SO₃ and an unchanged K.
A smaller amount of SO₃ and the same value of K.

questions.explanation: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, here backward, so there is less SO₃. For an exothermic forward reaction K decreases.

questions.stem: In which reaction is the catalyst homogeneous?

options.text: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), catalysed by iron
2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), catalysed by manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂
CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l), catalysed by H₂SO₄
C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), catalysed by nickel

questions.explanation: The acid mixes into the same liquid as the reactants: one phase, so homogeneous.

questions.stem: For the reaction X(g) ⇌ Y(g), K = 1.0 × 10¹⁵ at 298 K. Which statement about this reaction at 298 K is correct?

options.text: At equilibrium, the mixture is made up almost entirely of X.
At equilibrium, almost all of X has been converted into Y.
At equilibrium, X and Y are present in similar amounts.
The large value of K shows that equilibrium is reached quickly.

questions.explanation: K ≫ 1, so [Y]/[X] = 1.0 × 10¹⁵: the position lies far to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion.

questions.stem: Percentage of NH₃ in the equilibrium mixture at 200 atm (illustrative values): 350 °C, 57% · 450 °C, 36% · 550 °C, 22%. Why do ammonia plants run at about 450 °C rather than 350 °C?

options.text: Because 450 °C gives a higher equilibrium yield than 350 °C.
Because at 350 °C the reaction is too slow; at 450 °C the yield is lower, but far more NH₃ is made per hour.
Because K for this reaction increases with temperature.
Because the reaction is endothermic, so it needs heat to go.

questions.explanation: A compromise: a lower equilibrium yield, reached much faster, gives a higher rate of production.

questions.stem: Which is the equilibrium constant expression for 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) ⇌ 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g)?

options.text: Kc = [NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)
Kc = [NO]⁴ / ([NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵)
Kc = [NH₃]⁴[O₂]⁵ / ([NO]⁴[H₂O]⁶)

questions.explanation: Products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. All four species are gases, so H₂O(g) is included.
